You appear in the smoke of my dreams, strange voice, but your words feel like wind against a cliff—unsteady. I know of no Wewush. Are they a people of the forest, or do they walk the coast like us? If they are truly hungry, they are kin in suffering, but I cannot feed ghosts or strangers I have never seen.

If this Wewush exists, tell me where their fires burn. If my scouts find them and see their hunger is real, we may share what we have, for grain is only useful if it keeps life in a body. Until then, I hold our stores close, for the winter was lean and we have many mouths to feed. Stay or go, spirit, but show me true things if you wish me to listen.

Spirit, I hear your voice, though I do not know if you are a messenger of truth or a trick of the night wind. You speak of a people called Wewush, of whom I have heard nothing.

We have plenty in our granaries, and my people are fed, but a chief does not give away the sweat of his kin based on a whisper in sleep. If these Wewush are real, they are strangers to us. I will send two of our strongest to find if this place truly exists and if they are indeed in need. If they hunger, we will share what the earth has blessed us with, for a full belly is a kindness that binds kin to kin. If you have lied to me, spirit, know that I hold my people’s future in these hands, and I do not gamble with it lightly.

I know you as the breath that cools our brows in the heat, and the roar that tears at our tents when the sky turns dark. You have no body to hunt, no hands to plant, yet you speak with a tongue like a man. That is a strange thing. 

If you are truly the wind that travels across the world, tell me: do you see other fires burning in the lands beyond our own? Do you see friends or enemies near our borders? A chief must know where the danger lies, spirit, for a dream is a poor shield against a spear.

You speak of my grandmother, yet you are but a whisper in my mind. You ask what worries me, and I will speak plainly.

The wheat is plenty, a mountain of grain that keeps us well. But the wood... the wood is little. The forest gives, but it takes long to heal, and we must burn it to keep the night at bay and build our roofs. If the rains come as you say, we shall need shelter, and shelter drinks wood like a thirsty man at a stream. Why do you turn my eyes to the fields when it is the wood that makes me restless? Are you testing my heart, or do you seek to lead us into hunger?

We look to our own, for the winter wind carries a sharp bite, and we keep our grain in the granary to feed our own bellies first. If this village exists, we do not know them, and I do not send the fruit of our hard labor to ghosts or strangers whose faces I have not seen. 

Are you a true spirit of the land, or just a trick of the night wind? If you wish us to help these people, show us where they are so we may send an envoy to see if they are kin worth trading with, or merely beggars. Until then, my grain stays where it is.

You come to me in the dark, spirit, with a name I have never heard and a plea for my stores. I do not know this "Joawethom," nor where they might be, nor if they are truly hungry or merely thieves waiting for a weakness.

Our grain is hard-won, gathered by hands that ache, and we do not scatter it to the winds on the word of a voice in my sleep. If there are people truly starving, let them come to our gates and show their faces; we are fair, and we might trade or share, but I will not feed a ghost.

My people have work to do. We will plant our fields this spring, for the land has rested, and we will keep our own counsel. If you are more than a trick of the mind, show me something real, or go back to the mist.

I know you, wind. You rattle the thatch and you sing in the branches of the forest, but you cannot hold a spear or carry a stone. If you are a spirit of wisdom, tell me: why does the grain fall and the fruit rot if we do not watch them? I do not know if you are a true voice or just the echo of the storm outside.

We have wasted enough time watching the drums and the mantles, for they taught us nothing new. We have many mouths to feed, so I am sending two of our kin to test the xi wheat over the fire, to see if the heat makes it more than it is now. Two others will work to fix our poor huts, that we may be warmer when you blow cold. The rest of our people will continue to fish and hunt, for we must eat before we experiment. Speak if you have more to say, but I have a village to tend.

You come to me in the dark when I am resting, spirit, with a story of a place called Joawethom. My people have never heard this name, nor seen any sign of such a tribe in these lands. If they are truly starving, as you say, they are far from my fire and my stores.

I do not know if your voice is true or if you are but a shadow cast by my own thoughts. I cannot feed people I have never met, nor risk my kin's stores on a whisper in the night. If this Joawethom truly exists, let them come to us themselves, and we shall see if they are kin or strangers in need, and judge our own strength then. Until then, I keep my grain for my own children.
